newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -BTPs, bonos lose glitter on Buba fear.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -BTPs, bonos lose glitter on Buba fear.

text.p: Wariness that the German Bundesbank could raise interest rates in the upcoming months will take the shine off southern European bonds, despite remaining room for yield spread shrinkage in Italy and Spain, analysts said on Tuesday.
"If you look at the risk to return ratios, you should be selling rather than buying," said Julian Jessop, European economist at Nikko Europe in London.
"Above all it remains to be seen how the Club Med countries are going to survive if the Bundesbank raises rates."
The German central bank gave no word of its future monetary policy on Tuesday after a repo tender where there had been financial market speculation it could signal a tightening.
Analysts said they expected the bank to raise rates within three to six months, a move they said could undermine Europe's move toward a single currency.
Spain and Italy had been riding a wave of optimism about the European monetary and economic union (EMU) starting on time and with a softer criteria that would allow both on board.
BTPs, in particular, were being snapped up as it looked increasingly likely Italy would join the EMU.

Some analysts said there was still considerable room for Italian yield spreads with the Bund to shrink, but Jessop said that unless EMU were 100 percent certain, there were safer trades at the moment.
"People with overweight positions in Italy in practice are increasingly nervous, leading them to take profits now," Jessop said.
Some analysts said the Bundesbank uncertainty was a complicating factor for the short term, but in the medium term EMU would retake the centre stage of market decisions.

They said Italian bonds should outshine their Spanish cousins, but there is a risk the flashier BTPs could fizzle and burn out if the 1998 budget fails to convince the market that its spectacular deficit decrease would be sustainable.

"Italy on the short end is still incredibly attractive because it just hasn't caught up to the feeling that EMU is going to be a reality," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London. "But the market is going to be cautious."

The yield spread between the BTPs and Bunds has been swinging a bit wildly in the past week, widening out on Monday and Tuesday above 100 bp from 90 bp a week earlier, while bonos have moved more steadily in the 60-66 bp range.
The 10-year BTP/Bund spread was quoted at 104 basis points at 1415 GMT, and the bonos/Bund spread at 66 basis points.

Spain, with an almost definite chance of EMU entrance, was seen narrowing the 10-year spread between bonos and Bunds to 40-50 bp by the end of the year, analysts said. In Italy's case, where the single currency comfort level was somewhat less, the spread was seen reaching 65-75 bp.
Analysts see further wobbles ahead of autumn budget talks in both countries, but say Italy's budget will be more closely watched for psychological reasons.
"It's up to Italy at a political level to produce a budget that includes structural reforms. Spain has already done that to a large extent," said a fixed income strategist at a U.S. investment house.
Economists said Spain's budget framework, unveiled by Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato last Friday, was realistic and would underpin its drive to take part in the EMU launch.
